validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: strongly confirmed real, in-service infrastructure — not GEM-only. Independent corroboration from a trade journal (Oil & Gas Journal), an academic paper (Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, NG 155), an academic development-finance database (AidData/William & Mary, tracking the actual CDB/BOC syndicated loans), and an industry project database (NS Energy/Offshore Technology), none of which trace to GEM or to each other. CLASSIFICATION: correct — international natural-gas transmission trunk line (Fuel=Gas, PipelineType=transmission is the obvious correct call for a 1,200mm+ diameter, cross-border, multi-Bcm/y trunk line; no source suggests gathering/distribution/other). DUPLICATE: NOT a duplicate of P2299/P2300. The orchestrator's structural lead flagged that P1124/P2299/P2300 all carry LengthKnown=1833.0 and asked whether this is really the full Turkmenistan→Xinjiang SYSTEM length being repeated across three distinct-line rows (a defect shape). Independent evidence resolves this IN FAVOR of GEM's current values: (1) offshore-technology.com's own project page for Line C alone states 'Construction of 1,840km long line C' (i.e. an independently-sourced PER-LINE length, not a system total); (2) OGJ's article on Line C's 2014 start-up gives 'the length as 1,830-km' for Line C specifically; (3) thepeoplesmap.net states the THREE parallel lines (A+B+C) together have 'a total length of 5,511 kilometres', which divided by 3 is ~1,837 km/line — consistent with each line running an independent ~1,833-1,840km corridor, not one system total stamped three times. All three numbers cluster tightly around GEM's 1,833 km. So the repetition across P1124/P2299/P2300 is real (the three lines are built as parallel, near-identical-length corridors), not a copy-paste defect. This also explains gem.wiki's own citation #16 (IJGlobal, 'Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline Financing (3666KM)') — offshore-technology.com separately describes the ORIGINAL (Lines A+B twin-pipe) project as '3,666km long', which is exactly 2×1,833 — i.e. IJGlobal's figure is a twin-pipe (A+B built together) total, not evidence against the 1,833km per-line figure. Diameter further confirms P1124 is a genuinely distinct entity from P2299/P2300: Line C's diameter is independently and explicitly given as 1,219mm by AidData ('152 mm larger than Line A/B') and as '48 inches' (=1,219.2mm) by offshore-technology.com's Line C (Kazakhstan Section) page — both consistent with GEM's 1219mm on P1124 and with the roster note that P2299/P2300 (Lines A/B) are correctly 1,067mm/42in, a genuinely different, smaller pipe run in parallel. SPEC: Capacity 25.00 bcm/y for Line C is corroborated independently by OGJ ('reach 25 billion cu m annually'), offshore-technology.com ('25bcm annually...to 55bcm annually' system total), the OIES academic paper ('Line C, with a capacity of 25 Bcm, in 2014'), and AidData ('25 billion cubic meters per annum (designed capacity for Line C alone)') — 4 independent sources, exact match, tier=high. StartYear1=2014 is corroborated by OGJ ('Line C became operational...on May 31 [2014]'), AidData ('Operation commencement May 31, 2014'), and OIES ('Line C...in 2014') — 3 independent sources with a specific date match. One minor nuance for the record, not a correction: AidData separately notes an 'Official commissioning June 9, 2015' milestone for the Kazakh section (distinct from the 2014 first-gas/operational date), which explains why offshore-technology.com's aggregator field lists 'Operational Year: 2015' for the Kazakhstan-section-only entity — the two dates are not in conflict, they're different milestones (gas-flow start vs. ceremonial/official commissioning), and GEM's 2014 matches the more standard 'entered service' definition. Location: StartLocation 'Getaim' (also transliterated 'Gedaim') is confirmed as the real Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan border town where all three lines originate (Wikipedia infobox: 'Right bank of Amu Darya, Saman-Depe' in the same border area; multiple sources confirm 'Gedaim' as the border crossing); EndLocation Horgos/Xinjiang confirmed by OGJ ('enters China at Horgos, Xinjiang') and Wikipedia. FuelSource (Galkynysh; Dauletabad; Bagtyyarlyk gas fields) is corroborated by Wikipedia's Route section ('carrying natural gas from the Bagtyyarlyk gas fields...mainly supplied from Iolotan [=Galkynysh, the field's pre-2011 name] and Sag Kenar fields') and by the OIES paper, which independently names Dauletabad as a historic supply source for the Chinese route before Galkynysh came online. All independent, non-GEM, non-banned sources (no gem.wiki, abarrelfull, or theodora.com used as citations; gem.wiki citations were read only for leads).

validity.recommendation: Verify Owner3 = 'Uztransgaz'. Two independent sources describe the Uzbek-section joint-venture partner as 'Uzbekneftegaz' (the national holding company), not 'Uztransgaz' (its gas-transmission subsidiary) — consider changing Owner3 to Uzbekneftegaz, or confirm Uztransgaz specifically (rather than its parent) holds the equity stake before leaving it as-is.
validity.researcher_notes: Owner1 (China National Petroleum Corp), Owner2 (Turkmengaz) and Owner4 (QazaqGaz) are all well corroborated: offshore-technology.com's Line C (Kazakhstan Section) page states the Kazakh section is 'owned by China National Petroleum and National Company KazMunayGas' (QazaqGaz is the post-Nov-2021 renamed successor to the gas arm carved out of KazMunayGas to Samruk-Kazyna — using the current name is correct, per this project's own Egypt/China precedent of using current entity names). Owner3 'Uztransgaz' is the one soft spot: AidData's detailed project page for the Uzbek Section of Line C (record #54528) states the joint venture is 'Asia Trans Gas LLC...a joint venture of Trans-Asia Gas Pipeline Company Limited (TAPLINE) [50%] and Uzbekneftegaz National Holding Company (UNG) [50%]' — naming Uzbekneftegaz, not Uztransgaz, as the Uzbek equity holder. Wikipedia's infobox independently lists the same four-party structure but also names 'Uzbekneftegas' (not Uztransgaz) as the Uzbek partner. Uztransgaz IS a real JSC and IS Uzbekistan's gas-transmission operating subsidiary (gem.wiki's own dead citation, utg.uz/en/about/history/, now 404, was clearly trying to support exactly this), so this may be a holding-company-vs-operating-subsidiary naming choice rather than a plain error — GEM may intend the operating entity, which is a defensible choice — but I could not find an independent, live source that names 'Uztransgaz' specifically (rather than its parent Uzbekneftegaz) as an owner/equity-holder of this pipeline, so I'm flagging rather than fixing or citing it as confirmed. Not blocking existence/classification — filed as a caveat on this one owner slot only.

fills.researcher_notes: OGJ reports Line C entered service 31 May 2014; AidData's Kazakh-section project page confirms operation commencement the same date plus continued operation ('successfully transmitted gas to Khorgas on June 15, 2017'). Two independent, non-GEM sources confirming ongoing operating status.
Wikipedia (and every other source consulted) describes this uniformly as a natural gas pipeline system.

No source uses the literal word 'transmission', but classification as a transmission trunk line (vs. gathering/distribution) is unambiguous from scale/function: a 1,219mm-diameter, ~1,833km, cross-border, 25 bcm/y international export line described by every source as a major trunk pipeline connecting field areas in Turkmenistan to the Chinese domestic grid at Horgos.

summary: P1124 (Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline, Line C) is real and correctly classified — confirmed independently by OGJ, AidData, an Oxford (OIES) academic paper, and offshore-technology.com, none tracing to GEM. Not a duplicate of P2299/P2300 (Lines A/B): the shared 1,833km LengthKnown across all three rows is real (each parallel line independently runs ~1,830-1,840km) and Line C's 1,219mm diameter is independently confirmed as genuinely different from A/B's 1,067mm. Length/diameter/capacity/start-year all corroborate to GEM's exact values (tier=high). One attribution caveat: Owner3 'Uztransgaz' is unconfirmed — two independent sources name the parent holding company 'Uzbekneftegaz' instead as the Uzbek JV partner; flagged, not fixed, Owner fill left UNRESOLVED.
